audience.notes: Same adapted fears as the pillar and validity briefs. Fear A: 'a technical detail (the wrong witness, missing ID, someone who cannot follow the language) makes the marriage invalid or delays it'. Fear B: 'we pay for a beautiful wedding that turns out not to be a legal marriage, or paperwork breaks down between celebrant, registry and an overseas venue'. Paying parent: often asked to be a witness; wants to know they can, and that the marriage is recognised at home. Anti-persona: no witness-for-hire, 'cheapest' or 'quickest' framing.

payload.search_intent: Informational, quick answer first (how many, who), then depth. Secondary transactional intent in the SERP (hire a witness) is not ours to serve.
payload.angle: Two witnesses is the easy part. Give the official answer in the first 60 words, then cover what nobody ranking does: who can and cannot be one, what they sign, why NOIM witnesses are a different job, how the rules change in Italy, Greece, France and Bali, and who witnesses which ceremony when you marry legally at home and celebrate abroad.
spoke_rules: Cover ceremony witnesses only. NOIM witnesses get one short paragraph saying it is a different role with a different list of authorised people, then a link up. Do not repeat the pillar's NOIM witness list, remote witnessing detail, legal words, certificate types or the three overseas routes.

Link up to the pillar at least twice: in the first 150 words and in the NOIM H2. Descriptive anchors, e.g. 'everything else Australia requires before you marry' and 'who can witness your Notice of Intended Marriage'. Never the exact pillar keywords ('marriage licence requirements', 'marriage licence', 'notice of intended marriage', 'noim') as the whole anchor.

Legal facts only from the two research batches running now and facts already verified in the pillar (two witnesses, over 18 or appear to be, s 44 Marriage Act 1961, physically present, three certificates signed). Strategist has not researched new legal facts.
serp_gaps_to_win: Top results are witness-for-hire services, a 2021 US post that talks about a 'marriage license', and celebrant one-liners. A sourced, Australian, complete answer can win the head term.

'Who can be a witness' (PAA in all three cities, 50 searches a month): age, ID, understanding the language, whether family, parents, the photographer or the planner can sign, who cannot. Officially sourced.
NOIM witness vs ceremony witness confusion (a Melbourne marriage office mixes them): one clear paragraph.
Witnesses abroad: number, age, ID and language or interpreter rules in Italy, Greece, France, Bali. Nobody ranking covers it.
Legal at home, symbolic abroad: who signs where. Nobody ranking covers it.
Invisible work: getting two adults with valid ID to the right place on time across two countries, with a backup.

outline.h2: How many witnesses do you need to get married in Australia?
outline.answers: The search itself, in the first 60 words.
must_include: Opening answer: two witnesses who are, or appear to the celebrant to be, over 18, physically present with the couple and celebrant (s 44 Marriage Act 1961, AGD). Reuse pillar wording.
More guests are fine; only two sign.
Link up to the pillar within the first 150 words, descriptive anchor.
Key takeaways block (3 to 5 specific sentences) right after the intro.

outline.h2: Who can be a wedding witness, and who cannot
outline.answers: Who can you have as witnesses at a wedding? Can family be witnesses?
must_include: Family, parents, siblings and friends: what official sources say (batch A).
Who cannot or should not: the celebrant, anyone under 18, and any rule on understanding the language of the ceremony or needing an interpreter (batch A; only what official sources state).
Whether witnesses need ID or must give details on the certificate (batch A).
Practical line: choose two people who will definitely be there, sober and on time, plus a named backup.

outline.h2: What your witnesses actually do and sign
must_include: Watch the legal words and vows, then sign the three marriage certificates with the couple and celebrant (pillar fact; one or two lines, no repeat of the legal words).
What details of theirs appear on the paperwork (batch A).
Choreography: where they stand, when they sign, how to fold the signing into the ceremony and photos without losing the moment.
PAA 'Is being a witness at a wedding important': short, warm answer.

outline.h2: Witnessing your NOIM is a different job
outline.answers: Clears up NOIM witness vs ceremony witness confusion.
must_include: One paragraph: the NOIM is signed before an authorised witness from a set list, not your friends; a different list applies overseas. No list here.
Second link up to the pillar with a descriptive anchor, e.g. 'who can witness your Notice of Intended Marriage'.

outline.h2: Wedding witnesses when you marry abroad
outline.answers: How many witnesses, and what rules, in the destinations Australian couples choose.
must_include: Table: destination | witnesses required | age | ID or passport | language or interpreter rule | official source | our guide.

outline.h2: Legal at home, celebration abroad: who witnesses which ceremony
outline.answers: If we marry legally in Australia first, who needs to be there, and does the ceremony abroad need witnesses?
must_include: Legal ceremony at home needs the two adult witnesses; the symbolic ceremony abroad has no legal witnesses, so the honour can go to anyone, including people under 18 or people who cannot travel to the legal one (frame carefully; no legal claim beyond batch facts).
Ideas for honouring symbolic 'witnesses' abroad (reading, signing a keepsake certificate), clearly labelled as non-legal.
Link: /destination-weddings/civil-ceremony-in-italy-vs-catholic-and-symbolic-rites with a descriptive anchor.

outline.h2: Getting your witnesses there: the planning nobody sees
outline.answers: Invisible-work section; answers fear A and B. Ends with the advisor role.
must_include: Witness logistics for a destination wedding: passports valid for travel, any ID details needed in advance by the overseas registry, arrival before the civil appointment, interpreter booked if required, a backup witness already in the guest list, wet-weather or venue change that moves the signing table.
Room blocks and transfers so both witnesses are on site the morning of the ceremony.
Where a Wedded Advisor helps (brand-profile framing only, no prices): collecting witness details for the registry, aligning their travel with the legal appointment, briefing them.
One line on /wedded-world (no ticket push).
Closing discovery_call CTA.
